query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing 10–25 at.% of Mo with V in the NbZrTiHfMo alloy will improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance by reducing the electronegativity difference and modifying local lattice distortions, thus facilitating dislocation glide without compromising the solid-solution strengthening that underpins high yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa, whose high Mo content leads to an increased electronegativity difference and reduced plasticity.
generation.intervention: Substitute a moderate fraction of Mo (on the order of 10–25 atomic percent) with Vanadium to form alloys denoted as NbZrTiHfMo1–xVx, with x between 0.10 and 0.25.
generation.conditions: Room temperature deformation under compressive loading; the alloy must retain a disordered BCC structure; controlled processing to ensure homogeneity and phase stability.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and modified solute/dislocation interactions. The introduction of V alters the local atomic environment by reducing the overall electronegativity difference and increasing atomic volume misfits, thus modulating dislocation pinning and motion.
generation.mechanism: By substituting Mo with V, the alloy experiences a reduced electronegativity mismatch that lowers abrupt local stress fields. The V atoms produce larger volume misfits, which enhance lattice fluctuations that facilitate dislocation movement (thereby improving plasticity) while still contributing to solid-solution strengthening. This balance minimizes excessive dislocation pinning that otherwise hinders plastic flow.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to show improved ductility (i.e., higher plastic strain before failure) and a similar or only slightly reduced compressive yield strength relative to the unmodified NbZrTiHfMo alloy, thereby achieving a better strength–plasticity balance.
generation.baseline: Performance of the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy, with a compressive yield strength of about 1719 MPa and limited plasticity at room temperature.
generation.boundary: Improvements should be observed only within the moderate substitution range (approximately 10–25 at.% V). Beyond this range, phase stability (i.e., retention of the disordered BCC structure) may be compromised, or the strengthening mechanism might deteriorate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative change in compressive yield strength and plastic strain is uncertain due to the complex interplay between lattice distortion, solute-solute interactions, and dislocation dynamics. Optimization of V content is critical, and minor trade-offs in yield strength may occur.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbZrTiHfMo1–xVx alloys with x = 0, 0.10, 0.20, and 0.25 via controlled processing routes to ensure a disordered BCC structure. Characterize the phase stability with X-ray diffraction and microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM). Perform room-temperature compressive tests to measure yield strength and plastic strain to failure.
measurements: XRD phase confirmation of BCC structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the V-substituted alloys either significantly lose strength (exceeding a 10% reduction in yield strength relative to the baseline) or fail to show a notable increase in plasticity (if the improvement in plastic strain is not statistically significant compared to the baseline), or if phase instability (e.g., secondary phases) is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In random alloys, the disordered arrangement of solutes raises the interaction energy between dislocations and local solute concentration fluctuations. Dislocations are pinned in regions of favorable fluctuations, which are associated with high potential barriers to dislocation motion that can be overcome by applying high stresses and/or high temperatures. Yin et al. [] found that V can improve the mechanical properties of FCC HEAs based on the theory of interaction energy between dislocations and solutes in random alloys. The addition of V to the Cantor alloy family was calculated to predict the large volume misfits that are more capable of producing high strength relative to other alloying elements, and this prediction was experimentally demonstrated in the CoCrFeMnNi alloy []. Based on the material parameters in the solid solution strengthening model for each alloy, the addition of V is capable of producing large atomic volume misfits in FCC alloys, and thus, V can be a suitable enhancing element in FCC HEAs []. cited_evidence.kind: web:Electronegativity difference versus ideal mixing entropy in 3d CCAs
cited_evidence.text: There are several interesting points in diagram Fig. 4a. First, in spite of its lower chemical complexity, CrCoNi (Δχ = 0.100) has a higher solid-solution strengthening than CrMnFeCoNi (Δχ = 0.080). This is consistent with a previous observation that CrCoNi exhibits higher yield strength than CrMnFeCoNi. Second, FeMn, basis for many commercially used iron-manganese steels, is located at a very low position (Δχ ≈ 0.020). This implies good potential to develop a 3d CCA with very high strength if we optimize the plasticity mechanisms of CCA with high Δχ. Third, mixing entropy, one of the key properties of HEAs (a subclass of CCAs), is not strongly correlated with the electronegativity difference and thus with high solid-solution strengthening per se. Furthermore, there is a region in which the mixing entropy should be decreased to obtain greater solid-solution strengthening effects. Mixing entropy does not include information about the difference among the constituting elements, i.e., differences in local atomic configurations.
